`drmTMB` fits distributional regression models for one or two responses. Start
here if you have one response and want to ask whether predictors change its
average, its residual variability, or both. This article fits a small Gaussian
model, prints and reads its `summary()`, checks the fit with `check_drm()`, and
points to the next guide for your data.

The workflow has three steps: write one formula for each parameter you want to
estimate, fit the simplest model that answers the question, and check the fit
before interpreting it. If you instead have a phylogenetic tree, begin with
[Phylogenetic mixed models](phylogenetic-models.html). If your response is an
effect size with known sampling variance or covariance, begin with
[Mean effects and residual heterogeneity](meta-analysis.html). The broader
map, including other response types, is [What can I fit today?](model-map.html).

This vignette describes `drmTMB` 0.7.1, the current development version;
0.7.0 is on CRAN. Installation instructions, including the compiler toolchain
TMB needs, are on the [package home page](https://itchyshin.github.io/drmTMB/).

## Parameter names used in these guides

Each distributional parameter has one formula name and one plain-English name.
The guides use these names consistently:

| Formula name | Name in these guides | What it describes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `mu` (`mu1`, `mu2` for two responses) | location | Where the response distribution sits. For a Gaussian response, `mu` is the expected response, and its coefficients read like `lm()` or `lmer()` coefficients. |
| `sigma` (`sigma1`, `sigma2`) | scale | How far observations spread around `mu`. For a Gaussian response, `sigma` is the residual standard deviation (SD), modelled on the log scale. |
| `nu` and other family-specific names | shape | Features beyond location and scale, such as Student-t tail weight (`nu`). Gaussian models have none. |
| `zi`, `hu` | zero inflation, hurdle | The probability of an extra zero (`zi`) or of a zero from a separate hurdle process (`hu`). |
| `rho12` | residual correlation (coscale) | How two responses vary together within an observation after their `mu` and `sigma` models are accounted for. Only bivariate models have it. |

A family exposes only the parameters it defines: a Gaussian model has `mu`
and `sigma`, whereas a Poisson model has `mu`, plus `zi` when you model zero
inflation.

## If you already use lme4 or glmmTMB

The mean formula is written exactly as in `lme4` or `glmmTMB`, including
random-effect terms such as `(1 | site)`. Each additional parameter gets its
own formula, named by the parameter. The `sigma` formula plays the role of
`glmmTMB`'s `dispformula` for a Gaussian model:

```r
# glmmTMB
glmmTMB::glmmTMB(y ~ x + (1 | site), dispformula = ~ x, data = dat)

# drmTMB: the same model
drmTMB(bf(y ~ x + (1 | site), sigma ~ x), family = gaussian(), data = dat)
```

`bf()` is a short alias for `drm_formula()`; the name and the
one-formula-per-parameter layout follow `brms::bf()` (Bürkner 2017). For
worked side-by-side fits against `lm()`, `lme4`, `glmmTMB`, `metafor`, and
other packages, see
[Comparing drmTMB with other packages](comparing-with-other-packages.html).

## Fit your first model

Start with a Gaussian location-scale model when the response is continuous and
the scientific question is about both the expected value and its
predictability. In the example below, habitat and temperature change mean
growth, and habitat also changes the residual SD:

```text
growth_i ~ Normal(mu_i, sigma_i^2)
mu_i        = beta_0 + beta_1 grassland_i + beta_2 temperature_i
log(sigma_i) = gamma_0 + gamma_1 grassland_i
```

Here `i` indexes observations, `grassland_i` is 1 for grassland and 0 for
forest, the `beta` coefficients belong to the `mu` formula, and the `gamma`
coefficients belong to the `sigma` formula. The simulation sets
`beta = (1, 0.6, 0.4)` and `gamma = (-0.5, 0.45)`, so you can check whether
the fit recovers them:

```{r first-model-data}
set.seed(1)
n <- 120
dat <- data.frame(
  habitat = factor(rep(c("forest", "grassland"), each = n / 2)),
  temperature = rnorm(n)
)
mu <- 1 + 0.6 * (dat$habitat == "grassland") + 0.4 * dat$temperature
sigma <- exp(-0.5 + 0.45 * (dat$habitat == "grassland"))
dat$growth <- rnorm(n, mean = mu, sd = sigma)
```

The model has one formula for `mu` (the unnamed `growth ~ ...` formula) and one
for `sigma`:

```{r first-model-fit}
fit <- drmTMB(
  drm_formula(growth ~ habitat + temperature, sigma ~ habitat),
  family = gaussian(),
  data = dat
)
```

### Check the fit

Run `check_drm()` before reading any estimate. It reports one row per check:
optimizer convergence, the size of the final gradient, whether the Hessian is
positive definite, whether standard errors are finite, whether rows were
dropped, whether fitted scales are positive, and, for models with random
effects, whether groups are replicated enough and whether parameters sit on a
boundary:

```{r first-model-check}
check_drm(fit)
```

A clean fit looks like the header line above: every check is `ok`, with zero
notes, warnings, and errors. Read the `message` column of any `note`; resolve a
`warning` or `error` before treating the estimates as stable. The
[errors, warnings, and convergence guide](convergence.html) explains what to
try next.

### Read the summary

```{r first-model-summary}
summary(fit)
```

The first table has one row per coefficient, labelled by parameter:

1. Rows beginning with `mu:` are the `beta` coefficients, on the response
   scale. `mu:temperature` is the change in expected growth per unit of
   temperature, read exactly like an `lm()` slope.
2. Rows beginning with `sigma:` are the `gamma` coefficients, on the log-SD
   scale. `sigma:habitatgrassland` is the log of the ratio of grassland to
   forest residual SD.

The second table, `fitted:sigma`, gives the mean, minimum, and maximum of the
fitted residual SDs across observations, on the response scale. `logLik` is
the maximised log-likelihood, and `convergence: 0` repeats the optimizer code
that `check_drm()` already inspected.

Compare the estimates with the simulated values: the `mu` rows should be close
to 1, 0.6, and 0.4, and the `sigma` rows close to -0.5 and 0.45, each within
about two standard errors. A different seed gives different estimates; the
truth is a target for the method on average, not for any single data set.

Because `sigma` coefficients are on the log scale, exponentiate them before
reporting. `exp(gamma_1)` is the ratio of grassland to forest residual SD, and
`exp(2 * gamma_1)` is the ratio of residual variances:

```{r first-model-interpret}
sigma_habitat <- coef(fit, "sigma")["habitatgrassland"]
data.frame(
  residual_sd_ratio = exp(sigma_habitat),
  residual_variance_ratio = exp(2 * sigma_habitat)
)
```

For a fuller walkthrough of fitted means, residual SDs, residual variances, and
intervals, read [When variance carries signal, Part 1](location-scale.html).
Continue to [Part 2](location-scale-scale.html) when a predictor should change
the SD of a random effect. That model uses an `sd()` formula: `sd(site) ~ x`
says that the among-site SD of the `(1 | site)` intercepts depends on the
site-level predictor `x`.

## Choose your next guide

The first fit above is the right next step when your response is continuous and
you want to model its average and residual variation. Choose another guide only
when your data require it.

| If your question is... | Continue with | Key distinction |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Which response family fits continuous, count, proportion, robust, or zero-heavy data? | [Choosing response families](distribution-families.html) | A family determines what `mu`, `sigma`, and any extra parameters mean. |
| Do related species, sites, animals, or a supplied relationship matrix share deviations? | [Structural dependence overview](structural-dependence.html) | A structured deviation is not the same as residual variation or residual correlation. |
| Do two responses remain correlated after their means and residual SDs are modelled? | [Residual correlation with rho12](bivariate-coscale.html) | `rho12` is a residual correlation, not a correlation among groups or species. |
| Do effect sizes come with known sampling variances or covariance? | [Mean effects and residual heterogeneity](meta-analysis.html) | This is a Gaussian known-variance analysis, not a family for raw observations. |
| Is an estimate or interval safe to report? | [Can I fit and report this model?](capability-and-limits.html) | A model that fits can still have weak diagnostics or unsupported uncertainty. |
| How does my `lme4`, `glmmTMB`, or `metafor` model translate? | [Comparing drmTMB with other packages](comparing-with-other-packages.html) | Side-by-side fits of the same model in both packages. |

Use [What can I fit today?](model-map.html) when you need a compact
route-and-limitation map.

## Name the quantity before reporting it

Before reporting a number, name the estimand, the quantity the number
estimates. Four quantities can all involve a predictor `x`, but they answer
different biological questions:

- A `mu` slope, from `y ~ x`, is the change in the expected response per unit
  of `x`.
- A `sigma` slope, from `sigma ~ x`, is the change in log residual SD per unit
  of `x`.
- A random-slope SD, from `(0 + x | group)` in the `mu` formula, is how much
  the `x` slope (a reaction norm) varies among groups.
- An `sd()` slope, from `sd(group) ~ x_group`, is how a group-level predictor
  changes the SD of the group intercepts.

## Keep residual and group-level correlations separate

A bivariate residual correlation `rho12` describes how two responses vary
together within an observation after their `mu` and `sigma` models are
accounted for.

A random-effect correlation describes something else: how group-level
deviations, such as site intercepts and site slopes, vary together.
Phylogenetic and spatial correlations are further group-level correlations,
structured by a tree or by coordinates. Report each as its own quantity. If
correlation is your scientific question, continue with the
[structural dependence overview](structural-dependence.html) before adding it to
this introductory model.

## Next steps

Use [Can I fit and report this model?](capability-and-limits.html) for the
current reporting boundary for each model, and the [model map](model-map.html)
for syntax detail. Once this first fit is checked, continue with
[Checking and using fitted models](https://itchyshin.github.io/drmTMB/articles/model-workflow.html),
or choose a scientific question from the "Choose your next guide" table above.

Working in Julia? The DRModels.jl
[first-model page](https://itchyshin.github.io/DRModels.jl/stable/getting-started)
is the Julia starting point, and its
[R and Julia vocabulary page](https://itchyshin.github.io/DRModels.jl/stable/rosetta)
maps `drmTMB` syntax to Julia syntax. Its first example uses different
simulated data from this article, so compare syntax rather than numbers. Julia
is optional for `drmTMB` users.
